--- title: "Checking a fit" description: "A search that went wrong still prints coefficients. Three failures, stopping early, having no lowest point and changing from run to run, each leave a sign you can check for." order: 6 categories: [optimisation, reproducibility] --- ## A failed fit still prints coefficients [Finding the parameters](parameter-estimation.qmd) split models into those solved by a formula and those found by a search. A search can go wrong, and when it does the model still returns coefficients, a summary and predictions, all of them plausible. Nothing about the output looks broken. This page shows three ways a search goes wrong on the survey, the sign each one leaves, and a short list of checks to run before reading any coefficient. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Three ways a search goes wrong 1. **It stopped early.** The search ran out of steps and returned wherever it had got to. 2. **There was no lowest point.** The objective kept falling in one direction, so the search kept going until a limit stopped it. 3. **It gives a different answer each run.** Some methods make random choices while fitting, so two runs on the same data give two models. ::: {.diagram} ![A search can stop before the lowest point, walk off towards a lowest point that does not exist, or land somewhere slightly different on each run. Each one still prints coefficients and predictions.](img/three-failures.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Stopped early, ran out of steps, converged equals false: a U-shaped objective with a row of dots stepping down one side and stopping partway, short of the lowest point, which is marked with a cross; the coefficients look normal. No lowest point, the objective keeps falling, huge coefficient and huge error: a curve that falls towards a level it never reaches, with dots along it and an arrow labelled keeps going; the search walks off until a limit stops it. Different each run, random choices in the fit, no seed and no repeat: a row of dots for runs with no seed, spread along a scale of test error, with a bracket labelled spread; a seed repeats one answer but does not remove the spread. A note says each one still prints coefficients and predictions, so check for it."} ::: ## Worked example ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() d <- survey |> select(abundance, present, catch_weight_kg, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3, salinity_psu, substrate, season) |> drop_na() ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import statsmodels.api as sm from scipy.optimize import minimize from scipy.stats import poisson from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() d = survey[["abundance", "present", "catch_weight_kg", "depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season"]].dropna() # glm() models the second level of a factor, and present's second level is # "no", so the R fits on this page predict absence. We do the same, so the # signs match. absent = (d["present"] == "no").astype(float) ``` ::: ::: ### A search that stopped early `glm()` searches step by step and stops after 25 steps at most. We fit logistic regression for presence twice: once allowed only two steps, and once left to finish. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} stopped_early <- glm(present ~ chlorophyll_mg_m3 + depth_m, data = d, family = binomial, control = glm.control(maxit = 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> Warning: glm.fit: algorithm did not converge ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} full_fit <- glm(present ~ chlorophyll_mg_m3 + depth_m, data = d, family = binomial) tibble( fit = c("two steps", "left to finish"), converged = c(stopped_early$converged, full_fit$converged), steps = c(stopped_early$iter, full_fit$iter), chlorophyll = c(coef(stopped_early)[2], coef(full_fit)[2]), depth = c(coef(stopped_early)[3], coef(full_fit)[3]) ) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 4))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|fit |converged | steps| chlorophyll| depth| |:--------------|:---------|-----:|-----------:|------:| |two steps |FALSE | 2| -0.3118| 0.0038| |left to finish |TRUE | 5| -0.3442| 0.0037|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} X = sm.add_constant(d[["chlorophyll_mg_m3", "depth_m"]]) binomial = sm.families.Binomial() stopped_early = sm.GLM(absent, X, family=binomial).fit(maxiter=2) full_fit = sm.GLM(absent, X, family=binomial).fit() pd.DataFrame({ "fit": ["two steps", "left to finish"], "converged": [stopped_early.converged, full_fit.converged], "steps": [stopped_early.fit_history["iteration"], full_fit.fit_history["iteration"]], "chlorophyll": [stopped_early.params["chlorophyll_mg_m3"], full_fit.params["chlorophyll_mg_m3"]], "depth": [stopped_early.params["depth_m"], full_fit.params["depth_m"]], }).round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | fit | converged | steps | chlorophyll | depth | |:---------------|:------------|--------:|--------------:|--------:| | two steps | False | 2 | -0.3118 | 0.0038 | | left to finish | True | 5 | -0.3442 | 0.0037 | ::: ::: ::: The fit stopped after two steps reports a chlorophyll coefficient of −0.312 against −0.344 for the finished one, 9% out. On its own it would look entirely reasonable. R does print a warning, but the table of coefficients carries no mark, and the one place the difference shows is the `converged` field, which you have to ask for. A search can also report success without having moved. On [Maximum likelihood](maximum-likelihood.qmd), `optim()` fitted Poisson regression with depth in metres and its square in the thousands. It returned the coefficients it started from and a code saying it had finished. We repeat that fit and compare it with `glm()` on the same inputs. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Xraw <- model.matrix(~ chlorophyll_mg_m3 + depth_m + I(depth_m^2), data = d) y <- d$abundance raw_optim <- optim(rep(0, ncol(Xraw)), \(b) -sum(dpois(y, lambda = exp(drop(Xraw %*% b)), log = TRUE)), method = "BFGS", control = list(reltol = 1e-14, maxit = 5000)) raw_glm <- glm(abundance ~ chlorophyll_mg_m3 + depth_m + I(depth_m^2), data = d, family = poisson) tibble( fit = c("optim()", "glm()"), `reports success` = c(raw_optim$convergence == 0, raw_glm$converged), `log-likelihood` = c(-raw_optim$value, as.numeric(logLik(raw_glm))) ) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 1))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|fit |reports success | log-likelihood| |:-------|:---------------|--------------:| |optim() |TRUE | -4408.9| |glm() |TRUE | -2396.5|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} Xraw = sm.add_constant(d[["chlorophyll_mg_m3", "depth_m"]] .assign(depth_m2=d["depth_m"] ** 2)) y = d["abundance"].to_numpy() # scipy fails here by overflowing, and says so, where optim() reports success. with np.errstate(over="ignore", invalid="ignore"): raw_optim = minimize(lambda b: -poisson.logpmf(y, mu=np.exp(Xraw.to_numpy() @ b)).sum(), np.zeros(Xraw.shape[1]), method="BFGS") raw_glm = sm.GLM(y, Xraw, family=sm.families.Poisson()).fit() pd.DataFrame({ "fit": ["minimize()", "statsmodels"], "reports success": [raw_optim.success, raw_glm.converged], "log-likelihood": [-raw_optim.fun, raw_glm.llf], }).round(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | fit | reports success | log-likelihood | |:------------|:------------------|-----------------:| | minimize() | False | nan | | statsmodels | True | -2396.5 | ::: ::: ::: Both report success, but the log-likelihoods differ by 2,012, and higher is better. `optim()` stopped at its starting point. The flag says only that the search stopped by its own rule; checking that the answer is good takes a second route to the same model, or a look at whether the parameters moved from where they started. ### An objective with no lowest point `catch_weight_kg` is the leaked column from [Information leakage](../02-marine-data/information-leakage.qmd): it is weighed from the same catch that was counted, so every station where the species was present weighs more than every station where it was absent. We use it to predict presence. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} separated <- glm(present ~ catch_weight_kg, data = d, family = binomial) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> Warning: glm.fit: algorithm did not converge ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> Warning: glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} round(summary(separated)$coefficients, 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|) #> (Intercept) 27.716 3074.802 0.009 0.993 #> catch_weight_kg -157.709 13515.391 -0.012 0.991 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(converged = separated$converged, steps = separated$iter) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> converged steps #> 0 25 ``` ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} # statsmodels warns of "perfect separation" here, yet reports converged. # errstate hides numpy's overflow warnings on the way, which say the same. with np.errstate(over="ignore"): separated = sm.GLM(absent, sm.add_constant(d[["catch_weight_kg"]]), family=binomial).fit() # scikit-learn's LogisticRegression gives no sign at all: its default penalty # (C=1.0) stops the coefficient from walking off, so it looks ordinary. default = LogisticRegression().fit(d[["catch_weight_kg"]], absent) pd.DataFrame({ "fit": ["statsmodels", "LogisticRegression()"], "coefficient": [separated.params["catch_weight_kg"], default.coef_[0, 0]], "std. error": [f"{separated.bse['catch_weight_kg']:,.0f}", "none"], "converged": [separated.converged, default.n_iter_[0] < default.max_iter], "training accuracy": [ np.mean((separated.predict() > 0.5) == absent), default.score(d[["catch_weight_kg"]], absent), ], }).round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | fit | coefficient | std. error | converged | training accuracy | |:---------------------|--------------:|:-------------|:------------|--------------------:| | statsmodels | -189.775 | 99,544 | True | 1 | | LogisticRegression() | -8.89 | none | True | 1 | ::: ::: ::: The coefficient is −157.7, its standard error is 13,515, and the *p*-value is 0.99. Read plainly, the table says catch weight is about the least useful input you could have chosen. The truth is the opposite: it tells present from absent at every station. This is called **separation**. When one input splits the two classes completely, moving its coefficient further from zero always makes the data a little more likely, so the objective keeps falling and has no lowest point. The search walks off in that direction until it reaches its limit of 25 steps. The standard error measures how sharply the objective curves at the answer, and far out along a nearly flat stretch it hardly curves at all, so the error becomes enormous too. The sign is a coefficient and a standard error that are both huge, with the error far larger. It is not weak evidence; it means an input gives the answer away. Look for that input, and in practice it is usually a leak. R's warning `fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred` points the same way. ### A different answer each run A random forest draws stations and inputs at random for each tree, so a forest fitted without a seed is a slightly different model every time. We fit one ten times on the same training stations and score each on the same test stations. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} split <- initial_split(d |> select(-present, -catch_weight_kg), prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) unseeded <- map_dbl(1:10, \(i) { forest <- ranger(abundance ~ ., data = train, num.trees = 500) sqrt(mean((test$abundance - predict(forest, test)$predictions)^2)) }) round(unseeded, 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 4.490 4.471 4.441 4.450 4.493 4.484 4.481 4.511 4.475 4.509 ``` ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} # max_features="sqrt" and min_samples_leaf=5 are ranger's defaults for # regression; scikit-learn's own defaults differ. features = pd.get_dummies(d.drop(columns=["abundance", "present", "catch_weight_kg"]), dtype=float) train_X, test_X, train_y, test_y = train_test_split( features, d["abundance"], train_size=0.75, random_state=123) def unseeded_rmse(): forest = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_leaf=5).fit(train_X, train_y) return np.sqrt(np.mean((test_y - forest.predict(test_X)) ** 2)) unseeded = np.array([unseeded_rmse() for _ in range(10)]) print(unseeded.round(3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [4.828 4.835 4.808 4.821 4.805 4.85 4.821 4.825 4.803 4.836] ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble(rmse = unseeded) |> ggplot(aes(rmse, 0)) + geom_point(size = 3.4, alpha = 0.6, colour = ml_palette[["orange"]]) + labs(x = "Test RMSE (animals)", y = NULL, title = "One forest, ten runs without a seed") + theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Test RMSE of the same random forest fitted ten times without a seed. The runs spread over 0.069 animals, and every one reported success.](reading-a-fit_files/figure-html/fig-forest-runs-1.png){#fig-forest-runs fig-alt='A strip of ten dots along a horizontal axis of test RMSE, from 4.441 to 4.511 animals. The dots lie close together with no single run standing apart.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: The ten runs range from 4.441 to 4.511, a spread of 0.069 animals. That is small, and it is still useful: two models whose test scores differ by less than this cannot be ranked on those scores, because refitting one of them could reverse the order. [Choosing a method](../03-supervised-learning/choosing-a-method.qmd) found its two count models too close to rank on one split. Setting a seed makes the forest return the same number every time. That is needed for a paper someone else can repeat, but it says nothing about whether the number is reliable. The only way to find out is to leave the seed out on purpose and fit several times, as above. ## Each failure has its own fix | Sign | What happened | What to do | | --- | --- | --- | | `converged` is `FALSE`, or a warning that the search did not converge | Ran out of steps | Allow more steps; if it still does not finish, rethink the model | | A huge coefficient with an even larger standard error | No lowest point: an input gives the answer away | Find that input; suspect leakage | | A different answer on each run | Random choices in the fit | Set a seed to repeat it; fit without one to measure the spread | | The objective grows with every step, or becomes `NaN` | Step size too large | Take smaller steps; [standardise the inputs](gradient-descent.qmd) | | Coefficients swing when a few stations change | Inputs that move together, a flat valley | Check how the inputs correlate; consider [a prior](map-and-priors.qmd) | ## Some mistakes print no warning The warnings R prints loudest are not a guide to the failures that matter most. Two examples from earlier pages print nothing at all. - When two inputs carry the same information, such as depth in metres and depth in centimetres, `lm()` quietly drops one and prints `NA` in its place, with no warning. - The stratified split on [Splitting the data](../02-marine-data/splitting-data.qmd) did not stratify the rare class, and gave no error. Only checking the result against what was asked for showed it. "Converged" also means less than it sounds. A search stops when a step changes the fit by less than a set amount, the **tolerance**, and each package chooses its own. Two packages fitting the same model can disagree in the third decimal place and both report success. Finally, every check on this page asks whether the search did what it was told. None of them asks whether it was told the right thing: a Poisson model of counts that vary far more than Poisson allows converges without complaint. [Distributional assumptions](../06-assumptions-limitations/distributional-assumptions.qmd) takes up that question. ### A checklist before reading the coefficients 1. Did the search converge? Check the flag, not the look of the output. 2. Is any coefficient absurdly large, or `NA`? 3. Is any standard error many times larger than its coefficient? 4. If the method is random, how far does the answer move on a second run without a seed? 5. Are the predictions possible: no negative counts, and no probabilities below 0 or above 1? The last check needs no statistics at all, only knowledge of the species and the survey, and it catches many real mistakes. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - A search that went wrong still prints coefficients, so check the **convergence flag**, not how the output looks. Stopped after two steps, the chlorophyll coefficient was 9% out and looked normal. - A reported success is not proof: `optim()` stopped where it started and still reported success. Check the answer by a second route. - A huge coefficient with an even larger standard error means **separation**, an input that gives the answer away, not weak evidence. - A random forest gave a different test RMSE on each unseeded run, spread over 0.069 animals. Differences smaller than that cannot be ranked. - **A seed makes a result repeatable, not reliable.** Leave it out on purpose to measure the spread. - Some failures print no warning at all, so check that each result is what you asked for. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Fit `glm(present ~ abundance, family = binomial)`. `present` is defined as `abundance > 0`, so abundance splits the classes exactly. Compare its coefficient and standard error with the `catch_weight_kg` fit. 2. Refit the ten forests with `num.trees = 50` instead of 500. Does the spread grow or shrink, and why would more trees change it?
